card_quote: Has seen many 'everything you know is wrong' books come and go; thinks most are reworded internet lists; default answer: no, and would not order it for the library without strong reviews. / Runs an adult reading group; wary of books that are 'too smart for their own good'.
how_read: Looked at it as an object first: title page, copyright page, contents, then the back for index and sources. Read Rounds 1 to 3 properly, then Round 7 in full because it's quotations, which is her daily work. Flicked through the rest, and went to the back matter last. Spent twenty minutes there.

w1_friction.note: Already a bit smug. 'Told wrong' by whom?
w1_friction.quote: 100 famous stories you’ve been told wrong

w1_friction.note: The ISBN says 'to add'. A proof left in a printed book. I can't catalogue it.
At least it says the pictures are AI. Better than hiding it.
w1_friction.quote: The illustrations were made with AI image tools.

w1_friction.note: 'For who always knows the real story.' There is a word missing, or it is meant to be cute. Either way, odd in the front matter.
w1_friction.quote: For who always knows the real story.

w1_friction.note: A cartoon librarian who says 'says who?'. I do that for a living and nobody asks me to stamp things. Pleasant, but a bit much.
w1_friction.quote: forty years at the reference desk of a big public library

w1_friction.note: One of the sources printed in the book is Wikipedia. And the rest only 'on the website'. A reference book should stand without a link.
Napoleon is the Hanlon page again. Two pages for one quote.
The contents say Dunning-Kruger is on 81 and the next on 83, and here on 83 is a kite in a Discovery Stories heading, numbered 31 again.
Stamp: TRUE. Text: Franklin never flew it. A reference librarian would have this on the errata list the first day.
w1_friction.quote: Franklin never flew a kite in a thunderstorm

w1_friction.note: Nobody believes 'meme' grew up with no author. The 'popular version' was invented to give the book another TRUE.
w1_friction.quote: take it for slang that grew up on its own

w1_friction.note: A second 71 under Names That Mislead inside Round 8.
Written as if by another author, in academic jargon, and the source is 'various laboratory studies'. I would never cite that.
Another invented 'popular version', that umami is a marketing trick. Pads out the TRUE count.
w1_friction.quote: a word made up to sell a seasoning

w1_friction.note: The page numbers in the surprises list are off. Hooke is given as 210, and in my copy it's at 214. Everything after the middle is out by two to four pages.
w1_friction.quote: Did Hooke publish his law as an anagram? p. 210

w1_friction.note: One editor read and checked a hundred entries drafted by AI. That is not a checking process I would put in a collection policy.
w1_friction.quote: Krishna Chagti, the editor, then read and checked them.

w1_friction.note: Asks for reviews on the last page and an email list. Fine for a seller, but it makes it feel like a funnel.
w1_friction.quote: Honest reviews, good or bad, are the only kind worth having.

w1_friction.note: Tried the index. Giffen Good is given at 231 and the answer is on 236. Same drift as the surprises page. And no entry for the kite or goldfish at all.
A missing space, and 'Abraham Kaplan and Abraham Maslow' wrapped onto a line of its own. Proofing.
Who is the editor to settle 100 stories in history and physics? No historians or scientists named. He is honest that not all of it works, I'll give him that.
w1_friction.quote: Not all of it works, and none of it is his alone.

w1_best.why: Crud, not crap, and that Sturgeon called it his Revelation. The sort of misquote I fix at the desk.
The one-watch line printed without a name in 1930, and 'Segal' being a made-up eponym. Good detective work.
Six downloads before the lawsuit, two by her own lawyers. Memorable and sourced.
Rousseau never wrote 'noble savage'. People are sure he did, so it makes a good reading group question.
Clausewitz and the fog, and that a translator supplied the phrase.

w1_flat.why: Newton and the apple, a second time. Two entries on one anecdote.
Napoleon page that duplicates the Hanlon page.
Umami and the straw 'marketing invention' view.
Einstein's Nobel, which every trivia book has.

w1_review.headline: A nicely made list that isn't ready to be a reference
w1_review.body: Round 2 and Round 7, on misattributed quotations, are the best of it and I'd put some of those on the reading group's table. But the back matter is not reliable: the ISBN is blank, the index and surprises page numbers drift off by the second half, and there are two pages (the kite that says TRUE and the goldfish with 'various laboratory studies') that no editor can have read. Bottom line: I'd wait for the corrected edition and good reviews before ordering it for the library.

w2_review_first: Nicely packaged, fun to flick through, and the quote ones are good. If a friend asked I'd say borrow it before you buy it, and don't trust the index.

w2_lost.why: The bullet-hole plane, and then the same plane again on the next spread. I stopped caring because it was the same point again.
Laffer and the napkin, then Laffer again. American economics isn't what I picked it up for.
Hanlon, then Napoleon, then same history. Two pages too many on one line.

w2_read_aloud.why: Everyone at the group will quote it with three items. The answer is four.
Twain gets the credit for everything, and the answer has real dates.
People say it as Goodhart's words. They aren't, and it's easy to fact-check.
Twain or Einstein, and the answer is neither. A good gotcha.
Red herring and the hounds. Everyone has been told the dog story.

w2_cut.why: The goldfish entry, in a different voice with no real source.
The Franklin page, which contradicts its own stamp.
Apple on the head, when the next entry covers the same anecdote.

w2_book2: A blank ISBN, more pages that nobody proofed, and an index and contents that don't match the pages.
